demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
# Margaret's Story

Margaret sits in the office with her hands folded tightly in her lap, the calluses on her palms worn smooth from years of welding work. At thirty-eight, she carries herself with the quiet competence of someone who has spent nearly two decades mastering a skilled trade. But something has fractured in her since last spring.

The accident happened on a Tuesday morning in April. Margaret was working on a structural steel project at a downtown construction site—the kind of work she'd done thousands of times before. She was welding a beam connection when her colleague, Danny, approached from her blind spot. The noise of the site, the heat, the concentration required—she didn't hear him coming. When she turned, the electrode she was holding caught his face and shoulder. The burn was severe. Danny spent three weeks in the hospital and still carries the scars.

Margaret had been cleared of any wrongdoing. The investigation showed Danny had violated protocol by entering the work zone without proper notification. But the investigation report couldn't undo what happened. It couldn't erase the sound of his scream or the smell of burned skin that seemed to linger in her nostrils for weeks afterward.

In the months that followed, Margaret stopped sleeping properly. She lies awake at night replaying the moment—not just what happened, but all the tiny variations of what could have happened differently. If she'd turned her head a fraction of a second earlier. If Danny had called out. If she'd been standing two inches to the left. Around 3 a.m., when sleep finally comes, she dreams of it happening again, except in her dreams the injuries are always worse. Sometimes Danny's face is unrecognizable. Sometimes it's not Danny at all, but her younger brother, whom she'd helped raise after their parents died.

She returned to work in June, thinking routine would help. It didn't. Now, whenever someone approaches her workstation, her entire body tenses. Her hands shake. Last month, she nearly struck a coworker who tapped her shoulder to get her attention. She'd spun around with her welding torch still in hand, her heart hammering so hard she thought she might collapse. The fear is disproportionate—she knows this intellectually—but knowing doesn't change the way her nervous system reacts.

What troubles her most is the guilt that sits beneath everything else, heavy and immovable. She tells herself that Danny forgave her, that they've even had coffee twice since he returned to work. But forgiveness from him doesn't seem to touch the place inside her where the guilt lives. She wonders if she deserves to feel safe, if there's something reckless or careless in her nature that this accident revealed. She's begun avoiding social situations, turning down invitations from her small circle of friends. She finds herself watching videos of welding accidents online, almost compulsively, as if understanding every possible way things could go wrong might prevent it from happening again.

The work itself—the thing she's loved since she was twenty years old—now feels dangerous in a way it didn't before. She still goes to the site, still does her job, but it feels like she's moving through the day with a part of herself held in reserve, braced for disaster. Her supervisor has noticed her productivity has dropped. She's noticed it too. The precision and flow that used to come naturally now requires enormous effort, as if she's operating with a significant portion of her attention locked in that moment last April, waiting for the chance to change what happened.
